title: BLOCKING B1/J1: canonical selection is an accidental origin hierarchy
evidence: PR-JUDGEMENT-REVIEW.html finding B1/J1, query_v3/resolver.py:274-313. PR#23 is FIX-FIRST on this item alone.

spec.description: Canonical selection collapses, in production's actual data shape, to LEXICAL ID ORDER. Because SISO person IDs are origin-prefixed, alphabetical order IS a source hierarchy: bk: < crates: < gh: < registry: < yt:. Nobody chose that hierarchy - it is an accident of prefix alphabetisation that reads as policy.
spec.context: The six defect fixes in 3d648aa did NOT touch this: the reviewer confirmed _canonical is BYTE-IDENTICAL across 7957503..3d648aa. Verified against the PR's own fixtures, not reasoned about abstractly: seed=[gh:lovelace] resolves canonical to bk:lovelace because both are live with no merged_into, so the lexically smallest wins. Worse, registry/curated rows were INTENDED to be preferred but lexically registry: loses to bk:, crates: and gh:. A 12-long merge chain resolved to bk:chain-1, a superseded row. This also confirms the earlier preliminary finding that the handoff packet describes a canonical policy the code does not implement. Determinism is not the property in question - DEFENSIBILITY is, and 'alphabetically first' is not defensible as a source hierarchy. Reviewer's suggested fix needs no new machinery: in _canonical, order by an explicitly ranked origin list before the lexical fallback, keep lexical as the final tiebreak so determinism holds, and emit the choice as an evidence record like every other decision. Cold independent review 2026-08-07, reviewer did not author either PR, read-only.
